title: Prepositions and particles

objectives.can: Read the prefixed and independent prepositions and the commonest particles, above all דִּי.
Recognise the commonest prepositions, conjunctions and particles.

explanation.summary: Small words hold an Aramaic sentence together. Some prepositions are single letters joined to the next word (בְּ, לְ, כְּ and the conjunction וְ), others are separate words such as מִן, עַל and קֳדָם. The commonest word of all, דִּי, does several jobs at once: it means 'who', 'which', 'of' and 'that'.

sections.heading: Prefixes and separate words
body: Four one-letter words are written as the start of the next word. בְּ means 'in', 'with' or 'by'; לְ means 'to' or 'for'; כְּ means 'like' or 'as'; וְ means 'and'. The corpus shows them as the Prefix feature on the word they belong to. You can see each in a real word: בְּחֶזְוִי, 'in my vision' (Daniel 7:2); לְגֻבָּא, 'into the den' (Daniel 6:17); כְּשֻׁם, 'according to the name' (Daniel 4:5); וְחֶלְמָא, 'and the dream' (Daniel 4:5).

Other prepositions are whole words: מִן 'from, out of, by', עַל 'on, over, concerning', עַד 'up to, until', עִם 'with', קֳדָם 'before, in front of', אַחַר 'after'. In the texts a separate preposition often comes with a pronominal suffix that is part of the word (as in קָדָמַי, 'before me'); the next lesson is about the suffixes.
A prefix may change the vowel of what follows or may be joined to another prefix. Do not worry if the letters look new: look for the preposition first, then the noun.

sections.heading: לְ marks the object
body: The prefix לְ has a use that has no English counterpart: it can mark the direct object of a verb, especially when the object is a person or a determined noun. In Daniel 6:17 the king commands, and they brought Daniel: וְהַיְתִיו לְדָנִיֵּאל. The לְ on דָנִיֵּאל is not 'to'; it marks Daniel as the one brought.

The same job can be done by a separate particle, יַת, with a suffix, as in יָתְהוֹן, 'them', in Daniel 3:12. With an infinitive לְ means 'to' (purpose), as in לְהוֹבָדָה, 'to destroy' (Daniel 2:24). So before you translate לְ as 'to', ask what it is attached to.

sections.heading: דִּי
body: דִּי is one of the commonest words in Biblical Aramaic, and it has four main jobs. It is a relative word: 'who', 'which', 'whom', as in Daniel 2:37, where דִּי begins the clause about the God of heaven who gave the king his kingdom. It means 'of' between two nouns, as in Ezra 5:17 (the previous lesson). It means 'that' after verbs of knowing and saying, as in Daniel 2:8, יָדַע אֲנָה דִּי, 'I know that'. And with other words it joins clauses with the senses of 'because' or 'in order that'; in Daniel 2:10 כָּל קֳבֵל דִּי is 'forasmuch as', 'because'.

To decide which, look at what follows. A noun or a noun phrase, with no verb of its own, points to 'of'. A clause with its own verb points to a relative ('who', 'which') or 'that'. A pair of words such as כָּל קֳבֵל before it points to 'because'. Grammarians describe these as one word with several uses, not several words.

sections.heading: Small words of time, condition and negation
body: אֱדַיִן 'then' and its longer form בֵּאדַיִן are the usual beginning of a narrative step. The prefixed בְּ here is part of the word and does not mean 'in': Daniel 6:17 begins בֵּאדַיִן מַלְכָּא אֲמַר. כְּעַן is 'now' (Daniel 3:15). הֵן is 'if' (Daniel 3:17). אִיתַי is 'there is' or 'there are', and takes suffixes, as in אִיתֵיכוֹן 'you are' (Daniel 3:15).

The usual negative is לָא, 'not' (Daniel 2:10: לָא אִיתַי אֲנָשׁ, 'there is no man'). A prohibition uses a different word, אַל, 'do not': in Daniel 2:24 Daniel says to Arioch אַל תְּהוֹבֵד, 'do not destroy'.

misunderstandings: The בְּ inside בֵּאדַיִן is not the preposition 'in'. The whole word means 'then', and אֱדַיִן without בְּ has the same meaning.
לְ is not always 'to'. It can mark an object (לְדָנִיֵּאל in Daniel 6:17) and it can introduce an infinitive of purpose.
דִּי is not always 'of'. Between two nouns it is usually 'of'; before a clause it is a relative or 'that' or 'because'. The next word often decides.
לָא and אַל are both 'not' in English but they do not replace each other: לָא denies, אַל forbids.

deeper.heading: Why one word does so much
body: Grammarians trace all these uses of דִּי to a relative word that originally meant something like 'that which'. A phrase like 'house of the king' was once 'house that-of the king', and other uses grew from the same root of meaning. The reading in Daniel and Ezra is easier if you take דִּי as a general link and let the sentence say which link is meant.

examples.analysis: בֵּאדַיִן is 'then', one word. The לְ in לְדָנִיֵּאל marks the object of 'they brought'. The לְ in לְגֻבָּא is the ordinary 'into the den'. דִּי links 'den' to 'lions': 'the den of lions'.

reading.why: Daniel is thrown to the lions and the king calls to him next morning. In five short verses are בֵּאדַיִן, the object-marking לְ, several uses of דִּי, prepositions with suffixes, and the king's question.

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: Then the king commanded, and they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions. Now the king spoke and said unto Daniel: 'Thy God whom thou servest continually, He will deliver thee.'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: And a stone was brought, and laid upon the mouth of the den; and the king sealed it with his own signet, and with the signet of his lords; that nothing might be changed concerning Daniel.

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: Then the king arose very early in the morning, and went in haste unto the den of lions.

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: And when he came near unto the den to Daniel, he cried with a pained voice; the king spoke and said to Daniel: 'O Daniel, servant of the living God, is thy God, whom thou servest continually, able to deliver thee from the lions?'
